title: A torus is a scheme-surjective quotient of a finite induced torus
statement:
Let $k$ be any field [def-weil-field] and $T$ a $k$-torus [def-sfb-tori-multiplicative-type], with group schemes and homomorphisms as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. There exist an integer $m\geq1$, finite separable field extensions $L_1,\ldots,L_m$ of $k$ [def-pc-field-extension], an affine $k$-torus $P$, and a homomorphism $\pi:P\to T$ surjective on underlying topological spaces. Here finite separable means finite-dimensional as a $k$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] and every element has a minimal polynomial with no repeated roots in an algebraic closure. Put $A=\prod_{i=1}^m L_i$, with componentwise operations and diagonal $k$-algebra structure [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. For every commutative $k$-algebra $R$ there are group isomorphisms
$$P(R)\simeq(A\otimes_k R)^\times$$
natural in $R$, where $P(R)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(\operatorname{Spec}R,P)$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], the tensor algebra is that of [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property], and $B^\times$ denotes the multiplicative group of elements of a ring $B$ having multiplicative inverses. Surjectivity of $\pi$ is a statement about scheme points; it does not assert surjectivity on $k$-rational points.

source.place: Proposition 12.63, printed p.251, with Lemma 12.61 and Definition 12.62. The displayed product of restrictions has the stated unit functor. A redundant factor L=k allows m>=1, also for the trivial torus.

proof.text: First check the finiteness hypotheses needed for character duality. By the torus definition, $T_{\bar k}\simeq\mathbf G_{m,\bar k}^r$ for some finite $r$. The map $k\to\bar k$ is faithfully flat by the field-extension lemma (with $D=k$), hence flat and surjective on spectra; the affine flatness criterion and the definition of an fpqc covering make $\{\operatorname{Spec}\bar k\to\operatorname{Spec}k\}$ an fpqc cover. The split torus is affine and locally of finite type, since its coordinate algebra is $\bar k[x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_r^{\pm1}]$, generated by the $2r$ displayed elements. Descent of affineness and of local finite type therefore makes $T$ affine and locally of finite type over $k$. An affine scheme is quasi-compact; by the definition of finite type this makes $T$ finite type. This also works for $r=0$, when the coordinate algebra is $\bar k$.

source.place: Tags 02L5 (lemma-descending-property-affine), 02KX (lemma-descending-property-locally-finite-type); apply to the algebraic-closure cover.

proof.text: Fix $k^s/k$ and put $M=X^*(T)$. The torus is of multiplicative type by its defining geometric split form, so character antiduality applies after Step 1. Scalar extension identifies the underlying group of $M$ with $X^*(T_{\bar k})$. The split-torus homomorphism calculation, with target rank $1$, identifies this with $\mathbf Z^r$. Choose coordinate homomorphisms $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_r:M\to\mathbf Z$ from such a basis, and add $\varphi_{r+1}=0$. Antiduality supplies a finite Galois extension $K/k$ inside $k^s$ through whose finite group $G=\operatorname{Gal}(K/k)$ the action on $M$ factors. Set $m=r+1$ and $N=\bigoplus_{i=1}^m\mathbf Z[G]$, with left translation on the basis indexed by $G$.

source.place: Proposition 12.63, printed p.251, with Theorem 12.23, p.240: finite-rank character module and finite Galois action.

proof.text:
Define $j:M\to N$ by its integer coefficients
$$j(x)_{i,g}=\varphi_i(g^{-1}x).$$
Additivity follows coefficient by coefficient. For $h\in G$,
$$j(hx)_{i,g}=\varphi_i(g^{-1}hx)=j(x)_{i,h^{-1}g}=(h\,j(x))_{i,g},$$
so $j$ is equivariant. If $j(x)=0$, the entries with $g=1$ give $\varphi_i(x)=0$ for $1\leq i\leq r$, hence $x=0$ by the chosen coordinates. Thus $j$ is injective. The zero extra coordinate makes $m\geq1$ even when $M=0$. This is the source's dual-permutation construction using copies of the regular permutation lattice instead of separate stabilizer cosets.

source.place: Proposition 12.63, printed p.251: dualize a permutation-module surjection; explicit regular-permutation version.

proof.text: Apply the unit-torus character lemma to $L=K$, and write $Q=Q_K$. Its character basis is indexed by $\operatorname{Hom}_k(K,k^s)=G$, and the Galois action is left translation through $G$. Take $P=Q^m$ and $L_i=K$ for every $i$. The finite product is affine by the affine fibre-product formula, is of finite type since the finitely many generators of its factor coordinate algebras generate their tensor product, and becomes a product of multiplicative groups over $\bar k$, so it is a torus. Restricting a character to the $m$ factors identifies $X^*(P)$ with the direct sum of their character groups: a character on a product is the product of its restrictions, since each tuple is the product of its factor inclusions. Hence $X^*(P)=N$ with the specified action. The full faithfulness in character antiduality now gives a $k$-group homomorphism $\pi:P\to T$ whose character map is precisely $j$. Its point functor is $P(R)\simeq\prod_{i=1}^m(K\otimes_kR)^\times$, naturally in $R$, by the representing property of the product and of $Q$.

source.place: Proposition 12.63 and Lemma 12.61, p.251; product character identity in Section 12(g), p.239.

proof.text: Over $\bar k$, antiduality identifies $\pi_{\bar k}$ with the diagonalizable-group map $D_{\bar k}(N)\to D_{\bar k}(M)$ induced by $j$. Since $j$ is injective, identify $M$ with the subgroup $j(M)\subseteq N$. The split diagonalizable quotient theorem identifies this map, up to that isomorphism of its target, with the faithfully flat quotient $D_{\bar k}(N)\to D_{\bar k}(j(M))$. In the affine coordinate rings its map is faithfully flat, so the spectrum theorem makes $\pi_{\bar k}$ surjective on underlying topological spaces. No saturation of $j(M)$ and no smoothness of its kernel is required.

source.place: Proposition 12.63, last sentence, p.251; Theorem 12.9(b), pp.234--235, for the split quotient.

proof.text: The projection $T_{\bar k}\to T$ is surjective: since $T$ is affine, its coordinate map is $k[T]\to k[T]\otimes_k\bar k$, faithfully flat by the field-extension base-change lemma, and then surjective on spectra. Given $t\in|T|$, choose $\bar t\in|T_{\bar k}|$ above it, and by Step 5 choose $\bar p\in|P_{\bar k}|$ with $\pi_{\bar k}(\bar p)=\bar t$. The image $p$ of $\bar p$ in $|P|$ satisfies $\pi(p)=t$ by the base-change square. Thus $\pi$ has exactly the scheme-point surjectivity asserted in the statement.

source.place: Proposition 12.63, p.251: scheme-surjectivity of the descended homomorphism; explicit field-extension test.

proof.text:
Put $A=\prod_{i=1}^mL_i=K^m$. The finite-product tensor isomorphism is
$$(\prod_iL_i)\otimes_kR\longrightarrow\prod_i(L_i\otimes_kR),\qquad (a_i)_i\otimes b\longmapsto(a_i\otimes b)_i.$$
It preserves products and the unit by checking pure tensors and extending bilinearly, so its underlying module isomorphism is a $k$-algebra isomorphism. Units of a product ring are exactly tuples of units: the inverse of $(u_i)_i$ is $(u_i^{-1})_i$, and an inverse tuple forces every component to be invertible. Taking units and inverting the displayed algebra isomorphism gives $P(R)\simeq(A\otimes_kR)^\times$. Every formula commutes with a $k$-algebra map $R\to R'$, giving the required naturality. This includes the zero test ring, whose unit group is trivial, and rank zero for $T$, when our construction still uses one factor.
